questions.title: PR interval and first-degree AV block
questions.question: A prolonged PR interval on ECG is the best indicator of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ventricular repolarisation is reflected in the ST segment and T wave (and its overall duration in the QT interval), not the PR interval. The PR interval instead spans from the start of atrial depolarisation to the start of ventricular depolarisation, so it says nothing directly about repolarisation.
explanations.B: Correct. The PR interval reflects the time taken for atrial depolarisation plus the delay imposed by the AV node before ventricular depolarisation begins. A PR interval prolonged beyond the normal 0.12-0.20 second range signals slowed AV-nodal conduction, the definition of first-degree AV block, making it the best available indicator of AV-node function among ECG intervals.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bundle branch block is reflected in a widened QRS complex (beyond 0.12 sec), not a prolonged PR interval. QRS duration and PR interval measure different parts of the conduction system — ventricular conduction versus AV-nodal conduction — and are not interchangeable signs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ischaemia is signalled by ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion, changes in the repolarisation portion of the tracing, not by the PR interval. A prolonged PR interval on its own does not indicate active ischaemia in any territory.

questions.learning_objective: State that PR-interval prolongation indicates AV-nodal conduction delay (first-degree AV block).

questions.title: ECG signs of ischaemia
questions.question: On an ECG, an inverted T wave is accompanied by which additional finding as a sign of myocardial ischaemia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. ST elevation signals a fully occluded coronary vessel progressing toward transmural infarction, not reversible ischaemia. Ischaemia and infarction are different mechanisms — subendocardial hypoperfusion versus a completed occlusion — and ST elevation belongs to the infarction side of that distinction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A prolonged PR interval reflects AV-nodal conduction delay, an entirely separate mechanism from ischaemia. There is no established mechanistic link between AV-nodal conduction time and the repolarisation abnormalities that ischaemia produces.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A deep, wide Q wave signals infarcted, electrically silent myocardial tissue — a sign of completed infarction, not the reversible ischaemic process. A small Q wave from normal septal depolarisation is a separate, unrelated normal finding.
explanations.D: Correct. ST-segment depression, together with T-wave inversion, is the classic reversible sign of subendocardial ischaemia. Ischaemia alters repolarisation (the ST-T segment) before it alters depolarisation (the QRS complex), because the subendocardial layer is most vulnerable to reduced perfusion and repolarises abnormally early relative to the outer myocardial layer.

questions.learning_objective: Name the two ECG signs of myocardial ischaemia and explain why they appear in the ST-T segment.

field_notes.keySource: bank p4, unkeyed but zero-corruption reconfirmed textbook standard is D

questions.title: VSD and Q wave (as taught in this corpus)
questions.question: According to this question bank's marked answer, ventricular septal defect (VSD) can be indicated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A prolonged PR interval reflects AV-nodal conduction delay and is not the finding this bank's answer key marks for VSD; PR-interval prolongation and septal-defect signs are unrelated ECG changes with different underlying mechanisms.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A deep Q wave is the sign of transmural myocardial infarction (electrically silent, infarcted tissue), not the finding this source associates with VSD. Confusing the two would conflate a septal congenital defect with an acquired ischaemic injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An absent S wave is not the option this bank's answer key marks, and no mechanism connecting S-wave absence to VSD is given anywhere in the corpus.
explanations.D: Correct, as printed in this corpus — with an important caveat. Two independent local question banks (this one and an unrelated Telegram-sourced bank) both mark 'absent Q wave' as the sign of VSD, so this is authored as the printed, cross-corroborated local teaching point. It is not, however, how mainstream cardiology conventionally describes VSD's ECG correlates (which more typically involve axis deviation in AV-canal-type defects), and neither source gives a mechanism for the claim — it is recorded as taught in this corpus, not asserted as an established general clinical fact.

questions.learning_objective: State what this bank teaches about VSD and Q waves, recognising it as a sourced, cross-corroborated local teaching claim rather than settled mainstream cardiology.
questions.author_notes: Standing ruling: VSD -> absent-Q-wave stays as printed with a one-sentence sourced note (LANE-BRIEF '106 all' correction). Independently corroborated by the Telegram addendum bank (Spot 34.2).

questions.title: Lead aVR's normal appearance
questions.question: Which standard limb/augmented ECG lead normally shows a fully inverted (negative) P-QRS-T complex?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lead II views the heart from a position roughly aligned with the mean depolarisation vector (down and to the left, toward the apex), so it normally shows an upright, positive QRS complex — the opposite of what this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. V3 is a precordial (chest) lead positioned over the anterior chest wall; it is not one of the standard limb/augmented leads and does not show a normally inverted complex — precordial leads typically transition from negative to positive complexes moving from V1 to V6.
explanations.C: Correct. Lead aVR views the heart from the right shoulder, roughly opposite the mean direction of ventricular depolarisation, which travels down and to the left toward the apex. Because the depolarisation wave moves away from aVR's exploring electrode, its P wave, QRS complex and T wave are all normally inverted — the one standard lead where full inversion is the expected, normal appearance rather than a sign of pathology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. V2, like V3, is a precordial lead over the anterior chest and is not one of the six limb/augmented leads; it does not show the normally-inverted appearance that characterises aVR specifically.

questions.learning_objective: State which standard ECG lead is normally fully inverted and explain why from the mean cardiac electrical axis.
questions.author_notes: The bank's own p4 option list (aVF/V3/lead II/V2) omits aVR entirely, which the concept record flags as an internally odd stem; authored instead with the correct standard option set (including aVR) on textbook ECG-vector grounds.

field_notes.keySource: standard ECG-vector fact, bank's own option list flagged as flawed (aVR absent); triage p4

questions.title: Limb-lead electrode colour convention
questions.question: In the standard limb-electrode colour convention, which colour is assigned to the left-arm electrode?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Red is conventionally the right-arm electrode colour, not the left arm. Placing a right-arm-coded electrode on the left arm (or vice versa) is exactly the kind of swap this colour convention exists to prevent, since it inverts lead I and distorts the whole limb-lead set.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Green is conventionally assigned to the left-leg electrode, not the left arm. Because the limb leads are defined by specific electrode pairings, mixing up the leg and arm colours would produce a lead configuration inconsistent with the standard 12-lead layout.
explanations.C: Correct. In the standard (AHA-derived) limb-electrode colour convention, the left-arm electrode is coded yellow. Colour coding exists purely to prevent misplacement, since swapping electrodes between limbs inverts the resulting leads in a way that is easy to overlook without a clear, consistent colour system.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Black is conventionally the right-leg (earth/ground) electrode in many coding schemes, not the left arm. The ground electrode does not contribute to any of the recorded leads, unlike the left-arm electrode, which forms part of leads I, II, and aVL.

questions.learning_objective: State the standard limb-electrode colour convention and explain why colour coding matters.

field_notes.keySource: standard convention, unkeyed by bank diff; triage p4

questions.title: QRS duration and bundle branch block
questions.question: A QRS complex measuring more than 0.12 seconds indicates which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heart rate is calculated from the interval between successive R waves (300 divided by large squares between them), not from QRS duration. A rapid heart rate and a wide QRS complex reflect entirely different measurements and can occur independently of each other.
explanations.B: Incorrect. First-degree heart block is defined by a prolonged PR interval, reflecting delayed AV-nodal conduction, not a widened QRS complex. PR interval and QRS duration measure different segments of the conduction pathway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Myocardial infarction is signalled by ST elevation evolving to a deep, wide Q wave, not primarily by QRS widening. A widened QRS complex can occur in structural heart disease generally, but a bundle branch block specifically, not an evolving infarct, is the standard interpretation of duration beyond 0.12 seconds.
explanations.D: Correct. Normal ventricular depolarisation completes within 0.06-0.10 seconds because the His-Purkinje system activates both ventricles almost simultaneously. A bundle branch block interrupts conduction down one bundle branch, forcing that ventricle to be activated slowly, cell-to-cell, from the other side — this widens the QRS beyond 0.12 seconds, the standard cutoff for a complete bundle branch block.

questions.learning_objective: State the QRS duration cutoff for bundle branch block and explain the mechanism of QRS widening.

field_notes.keySource: second-pass diff recovered key D; triage p10

questions.title: Heart rate from an ECG strip
questions.question: On a regular-rhythm ECG strip, there are 6 large squares between two successive R waves. Using the standard 300-divided-by-large-squares rule, what is the heart rate?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 85 beats/min does not follow from dividing 300 by 6; it would require roughly 3.5 large squares between R waves, not 6, so this figure does not match the strip described in the stem.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 75 beats/min corresponds to 4 large squares between R waves (300/4=75), not the 6 large squares stated in this question. Reading the wrong number of squares off a strip is a common source of this kind of error.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 60 beats/min corresponds to 5 large squares between R waves (300/5=60), one fewer than the 6 large squares specified here, so it does not match the given strip measurement.
explanations.D: Correct. Standard ECG paper runs at 25 mm/s, giving 300 large squares per minute. For a regular rhythm, heart rate equals 300 divided by the number of large squares between two successive R waves: 300/6 = 50 beats/min. This method only applies to a regular rhythm; an irregular rhythm requires counting R waves over a longer strip instead.

questions.learning_objective: Calculate heart rate from the large-square count between successive R waves.

field_notes.keySource: second-pass diff recovered key B (83, related item); worked corroboration Telegram Spot 31 (300/6=50)

questions.title: ECG calibration standard
questions.question: At standard ECG paper calibration (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV), one large square corresponds to which time and voltage values?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.04 sec / 0.1 mV is the value of one SMALL square, not one large square. Each large square contains five small squares, so its time and voltage values are five times larger than the small square's.
explanations.B: Correct. At standard calibration (25 mm/s paper speed, 10 mm/mV gain), each small square (1 mm) represents 0.04 seconds and 0.1 mV, and each large square (5 mm, made of five small squares) therefore represents 0.2 seconds and 0.5 mV. This calibration is what lets duration and amplitude be read directly off the ECG grid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1 sec / 1 mV would correspond to five large squares' worth of time and two large squares' worth of voltage at standard calibration, not a single large square; this option overstates both values considerably.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 0.1 sec / 0.2 mV does not match the standard calibration for either a small or a large square — it appears to mix values from the two square sizes rather than describing either one consistently.

questions.learning_objective: State the time and voltage value of one large ECG square at standard calibration.

field_notes.keySource: standard calibration fact, unkeyed by bank diff (diagram-dependent); triage p11

questions.title: Q wave and septal depolarisation
questions.question: Interventricular septal depolarisation is represented on the ECG by which wave?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The P wave represents atrial depolarisation, an entirely separate event from septal depolarisation, which occurs later, as the first part of the ventricular (QRS) complex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The R wave represents the bulk of free-ventricular-wall depolarisation, which follows septal depolarisation. It is the larger, later deflection in the QRS complex, not the small initial one associated with the septum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The S wave represents the final phase of ventricular depolarisation (the basal portions of the ventricles), occurring after both septal depolarisation (Q wave) and free-wall depolarisation (R wave), not the septum itself.
explanations.D: Correct. Ventricular depolarisation begins in the interventricular septum, activated from the left bundle branch before the free ventricular walls depolarise. This early, small, septal depolarisation is recorded as the small initial negative deflection — the Q wave — in leads that view the septum from the left.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Q wave represents septal depolarisation and distinguish a normal from a pathological Q wave.

field_notes.keySource: standard ECG-physiology fact, unkeyed by bank diff; triage p18

questions.title: Atrial hypertrophy and the P wave
questions.question: The P wave becomes enlarged (taller or wider/notched, depending on which chamber) in which condition?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ventricular hypertrophy increases the amplitude of the QRS complex, not the P wave, because the P wave reflects atrial, not ventricular, depolarisation. Ventricular and atrial hypertrophy are read off two different parts of the tracing.
explanations.B: Correct. The P wave represents atrial depolarisation, and its amplitude and duration reflect the mass and size of the depolarising atrial tissue. Atrial hypertrophy or enlargement — right atrial enlargement from pulmonary hypertension, or left atrial enlargement from mitral valve disease — increases this electrical mass, so the P wave becomes taller (right atrial) or wider/notched (left atrial, 'P mitrale').
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bundle branch block widens the QRS complex (ventricular conduction), a completely different part of the tracing from the P wave, which reflects atrial rather than ventricular electrical activity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. First-degree AV block prolongs the PR interval (the timing between the P wave and the QRS complex), not the P wave's own amplitude or shape. PR-interval prolongation and P-wave enlargement are distinct findings reflecting different mechanisms.

questions.learning_objective: State that atrial hypertrophy enlarges the P wave and name which chamber produces which shape change.

questions.title: Acute MI ECG evolution vs ischaemia
questions.question: Which ECG change is characteristic of an evolving acute myocardial infarction, as distinct from ischaemia without infarction?

options.C: ST-segment elevation evolving to a deep, wide pathological Q wave

explanations.A: Incorrect. T-wave inversion alone is a sign of reversible myocardial ischaemia, not an evolving infarction. It reflects altered repolarisation without necrosis, and typically resolves if perfusion is restored before infarction occurs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ST-segment depression alone likewise signals reversible subendocardial ischaemia, not a completed or evolving infarct. Ischaemia and infarction are different mechanisms — the former is reversible hypoperfusion, the latter is established tissue death.
explanations.C: Correct. ST-segment elevation signals a fully occluded coronary vessel and transmural injury; as the infarct evolves, a deep, wide pathological Q wave develops because the infarcted, electrically silent tissue generates no depolarisation current, so the recording electrode instead 'sees through' to the opposite wall. This evolution from ST elevation to a pathological Q wave is the hallmark of a completed, not merely threatened, infarction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A shortened QT interval is the ECG change seen in hypercalcaemia, an electrolyte disturbance affecting the ventricular action potential's plateau phase — it has no established relationship to acute myocardial infarction or ischaemia.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the ECG evolution of acute myocardial infarction from ischaemia without infarction.

questions.title: Hypercalcaemia and the QT interval
questions.question: What ECG change results from hypercalcaemia?

explanations.A: Correct. The QT interval spans ventricular depolarisation through the end of repolarisation, and its duration is set mainly by how long the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential lasts. Raised extracellular calcium shortens this calcium-dependent plateau, completing it faster, which shortens the QT interval on the surface ECG — the opposite effect to hypocalcaemia, which prolongs the plateau and lengthens QT.
explanations.B: Incorrect. QT-interval prolongation is the effect of hypocalcaemia (which prolongs the action potential's plateau), not hypercalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia moves the QT interval in the opposite direction — shortening, not lengthening, it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. PR-interval changes reflect AV-nodal conduction timing, which is not the mechanism by which calcium disturbances affect the ECG. Calcium's principal ECG effect is on ventricular repolarisation duration (QT interval), not AV-nodal conduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. QRS widening reflects a ventricular conduction problem such as bundle branch block or severe hyperkalaemia, not a calcium disturbance. Hypercalcaemia's characteristic ECG effect is specifically on the QT interval, not QRS duration.

questions.learning_objective: State that hypercalcaemia shortens the QT interval and explain the action-potential mechanism.
questions.source_citation: Practical CVS Qs Bank, ASM Minds, AU-MED-106 Physiology, Spot 16

questions.title: V6 electrode placement
questions.question: Where is the V6 recording electrode placed on a standard 12-lead ECG?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 4th left intercostal space parasternal position corresponds to V2, one of the septal precordial leads, not V6, which is placed further laterally and one intercostal space lower.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The 5th left intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, is the position for V4, the apical precordial lead, not V6. V4 and V6 sit at the same intercostal level but at different horizontal positions.
explanations.C: Correct. V6 is placed at the 5th left intercostal space in the mid-axillary line — the most lateral of the standard precordial leads, viewing the lateral wall of the left ventricle. Together with the other five chest leads, it helps the precordial lead set view the horizontal plane of the heart.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 2nd left intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, does not correspond to any standard precordial electrode position; V1 and V2 are placed at the 4th intercostal space either side of the sternum, not the 2nd space.

questions.learning_objective: State the anatomical landmark for V6 electrode placement.

questions.title: Ventricular hypertrophy and QRS amplitude
questions.question: In ventricular hypertrophy, what happens to the amplitude of the QRS complex?

explanations.A: Incorrect. QRS amplitude falling would be the opposite of what hypertrophied ventricular tissue produces; more, not less, depolarising muscle mass generates a larger, not smaller, voltage signal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. QRS amplitude does not stay the same when ventricular mass increases, because the summed electrical signal from ventricular depolarisation scales with the amount of muscle tissue depolarising.
explanations.C: Correct. QRS amplitude reflects the mass of ventricular tissue depolarising at any instant. Ventricular hypertrophy increases that muscle mass, so the summed depolarisation voltage — and therefore the QRS amplitude recorded on the ECG — increases correspondingly, distinct from QRS duration, which instead reflects conduction speed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. QRS amplitude becoming absent would imply no ventricular depolarisation is occurring at all, which is inconsistent with ventricular hypertrophy — a state of increased, not absent, ventricular muscle activity.

questions.learning_objective: State that ventricular hypertrophy increases QRS amplitude and distinguish amplitude from duration changes.

questions.title: Normal QT interval duration (disagreement recorded)
questions.question: What is the normal duration of the QT interval, as taught by this question bank's answer key?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.12-0.20 sec is the normal range for the PR interval, not the QT interval. Confusing the two intervals is a common error, since both are commonly-quoted normal ranges on the same tracing but measure different portions of the cardiac cycle.
explanations.B: Correct, as printed and independently corroborated. This bank's answer-key copy marks the normal QT interval as 0.3-0.4 seconds, and this exact value is independently corroborated by an unrelated Telegram-sourced bank's own printed key. The bank's own plain (non-key) copy shows '1-3 sec' in the same option slot, which is recorded as an uncorrected source-side typo rather than a genuine competing teaching value, since no independent source supports it and it is physiologically implausible for a QT interval.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.06-0.10 sec is the normal range for QRS duration, not the QT interval, which spans the whole of ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation and is therefore considerably longer than the QRS complex alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This value appears as an uncorrected typo in this bank's own plain (non-key) copy at the same option slot the keyed copy marks correct with 0.3-0.4 sec. A QT interval of 1-3 seconds is physiologically implausible (it would represent a profoundly prolonged interval far beyond any clinical long-QT syndrome), and no independent source in the corpus corroborates it.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal QT interval duration this bank teaches and recognise the plain copy's conflicting option text as a source-side typo, not a genuine disagreement.
